title: SQL Indexes & Query Plans: A Field Handbook
summary: A dense, practical guide to how relational databases store and search data — B-tree internals, composite index column order, covering indexes, reading EXPLAIN output, seq scan vs index scan trade-offs, and the cases where an index makes things worse.

chapters.title: Why Indexes Exist
points: Definition: an index is a separate, ordered, redundant data structure that maps column values to row locations, maintained by the DB automatically
Without an index the only access path is a full table scan: read every page, discard non-matching rows — O(N) work regardless of how few rows match
Table (heap) rows are stored unordered; insertion order, not value order — nothing about the heap helps you find WHERE email = 'x'
An index trades write cost and disk space for read speed: every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on an indexed column must also update the index
Selectivity = fraction of rows a predicate matches. Low fraction (1 row of 1M) = high selectivity = index-friendly. Matching 40% of the table = index usually loses
Cardinality = number of distinct values in a column. `user_id` on a 1M-row table has high cardinality; `is_deleted` has cardinality 2
The DB never guarantees an index is used — the query planner chooses at runtime based on statistics, and can change its mind as data grows
Rule of thumb: index columns that appear in WHERE, JOIN ON, ORDER BY, and GROUP BY — not columns you only SELECT
Primary keys get an index automatically in every major engine; UNIQUE constraints are implemented as unique indexes
Example: `CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users (email);` turns a 1M-row scan into ~3 page reads

chapters.title: B-tree Internals
points: Real DB indexes are B+trees: internal nodes hold only separator keys and child pointers; all actual keys live in leaf nodes
Leaf nodes are linked in a doubly-linked list, which is what makes range scans and ORDER BY cheap — walk sideways, no re-descent
Nodes are sized to one disk page (typically 8KB in Postgres, 16KB in InnoDB), so one node fetch = one I/O
High fan-out (hundreds of keys per node) makes trees shallow: 1M rows ≈ 3 levels, 1B rows ≈ 4-5 levels
Lookup cost is O(log_f N) page reads where f is fan-out — near-constant in practice because upper levels stay cached in RAM
The tree stays balanced on insert by splitting a full node and pushing a separator key up; deletes may merge nodes
Leaf entries store the key plus a row pointer: a physical heap TID in Postgres, the primary key value in InnoDB (clustered)
Clustered index (InnoDB, SQL Server) = the table data itself is stored in leaf nodes, in key order. Only one per table
Secondary index in a clustered engine stores the PK, so every lookup costs an extra PK traversal — keep primary keys narrow
Because the tree is ordered, a B-tree supports =, <, >, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE 'prefix%', ORDER BY, MIN/MAX — but not LIKE '%suffix' or arbitrary functions
Index bloat: deleted entries leave dead space; Postgres reclaims it via VACUUM or REINDEX

chapters.title: Other Index Types & When B-tree Isn't Enough
points: Hash index: O(1) equality lookup, no range support, no ordering. Rarely worth it over a B-tree
GIN (Postgres): inverted index for arrays, JSONB containment, and full-text search — one index entry per element, not per row
GiST: geometric/nearest-neighbour queries and ranges; supports operators B-trees can't express
BRIN: stores min/max per block range. Tiny on disk, only useful when physical row order correlates with the column (e.g. append-only timestamps)
Bitmap index (Oracle/analytics DBs): great for low-cardinality columns in OLAP, terrible under concurrent writes due to lock granularity
Partial index: `CREATE INDEX ... WHERE status = 'pending'` — indexes only rows you actually query, dramatically smaller
Expression/functional index: `CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email))` — required because `WHERE lower(email)=?` cannot use a plain email index
Unique index enforces a constraint and speeds lookups simultaneously; NULLs are treated as distinct in most engines
Comparison row — B-tree: ordered, general purpose, ~all queries. Hash: equality only. GIN: containment/text. BRIN: huge correlated tables
Choosing wrong: a GIN index on a plain integer column is slower and larger than the B-tree it replaced

chapters.title: Composite Indexes and Column Order
points: A composite (multi-column) index sorts by the first column, then breaks ties with the second, then the third — like a phone book sorted by (last_name, first_name)
Leftmost prefix rule: an index on (a, b, c) serves WHERE a, WHERE a AND b, WHERE a AND b AND c — but NOT WHERE b alone or WHERE c alone
Equality-first rule: put columns used with = before columns used with ranges. (status, created_at) beats (created_at, status) for `WHERE status='x' AND created_at > ?`
Once the index hits a range predicate, subsequent columns can no longer be used for seeking — only for filtering or covering
Example: index (tenant_id, created_at) makes `WHERE tenant_id=7 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20` a bounded index scan with zero sort
A composite index can replace several single-column indexes: (a, b) makes a standalone index on (a) redundant — drop it
But (a, b) does NOT replace an index on (b); if you need both directions you need two indexes
Column order also affects sort satisfaction: (a ASC, b DESC) supports `ORDER BY a ASC, b DESC` and its exact reverse, nothing else
Cardinality-first is a common myth — ordering by selectivity matters far less than matching the query's equality/range/sort shape
More columns = wider entries = fewer keys per page = deeper tree and bigger cache footprint. Keep composites to what queries need
Gotcha: an IN list on the leading column behaves like equality and still allows the next column to be seeked

chapters.title: Covering Indexes & Index-Only Scans
points: Covering index: the index contains every column the query touches, so the engine never reads the heap/table at all
Postgres calls this an Index Only Scan; SQL Server calls it a covered query; MySQL's EXPLAIN shows `Using index`
INCLUDE columns: `CREATE INDEX idx ON orders (customer_id) INCLUDE (total, status)` stores payload in the leaf without adding it to the sort key
INCLUDE columns cannot be used for seeking or ordering — they only satisfy the SELECT list, keeping the key narrow
Postgres index-only scans still consult the visibility map; if pages aren't all-visible it falls back to heap fetches — EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows `Heap Fetches: N`
Run VACUUM to refresh the visibility map and make index-only scans actually skip the heap
In InnoDB every secondary index implicitly covers the primary key, so `SELECT id WHERE email=?` is already covered
Best win: turning a query that reads 5,000 random heap pages into one sequential index range read
Cost: wider index, more write amplification, and any UPDATE of an included column now dirties the index too
Anti-pattern: `SELECT *` defeats covering by definition — narrow your column list first, then consider covering
Example rewrite: replace (user_id) with (user_id, created_at) INCLUDE (title) to serve a feed query entirely from the index

chapters.title: How the Query Planner Decides
points: The planner is cost-based: it enumerates candidate plans, estimates cost for each, and picks the cheapest — it does not follow your query's written order
Cost is an abstract unit built from I/O and CPU constants: in Postgres, seq_page_cost=1.0, random_page_cost=4.0, cpu_tuple_cost=0.01
Statistics drive estimates: row counts, distinct values, most-common-values lists, and histograms collected by ANALYZE / ANALYZE TABLE
Estimated rows × per-row cost = plan cost. A bad row estimate is the single most common cause of a bad plan
Stale statistics after a bulk load make the planner think a table is tiny and choose a nested loop over 10M rows
Correlated predicates break independence assumptions: `WHERE city='Paris' AND country='France'` is estimated as the product of two fractions, wildly underestimating
Fix correlation with extended statistics (Postgres `CREATE STATISTICS`) or by reshaping the query
random_page_cost tuned to 4.0 assumes spinning disks; on SSDs lowering it to ~1.1 makes index scans correctly attractive
Join order and join method (nested loop / hash / merge) are chosen at the same time as access paths — indexes change which joins are viable
Planner hints exist in Oracle and MySQL (`FORCE INDEX`), and via `pg_hint_plan` in Postgres; prefer fixing statistics over pinning plans
Plan caching / prepared statements can reuse a plan built for an unrepresentative parameter — 'parameter sniffing'

chapters.title: Reading EXPLAIN Output
points: `EXPLAIN` shows the estimated plan only; `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually executes the query and reports real timings and row counts
EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the statement — wrap DML in BEGIN … ROLLBACK before analyzing an UPDATE or DELETE
Read the tree inside-out and bottom-up: the most indented nodes run first and feed their parent
Node line anatomy: `Seq Scan on orders (cost=0.00..18334.00 rows=1000000 width=44)` — startup cost .. total cost, estimated rows, average row bytes in output
Startup cost is work before the first row emerges: 0 for a scan, high for a Sort or Hash build, which is why LIMIT favors low-startup plans
With ANALYZE you also get `actual time=0.021..3.140 rows=998 loops=12` — note total time is per-loop, so multiply by loops
Estimate vs actual mismatch (rows=1 vs rows=90000) is the smoking gun for stale or missing statistics
`Rows Removed by Filter: N` means the DB read rows and threw them away — a missing or wrongly-ordered index
Use `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` to see shared hits vs reads — the real I/O story that cost numbers only approximate
MySQL: `EXPLAIN` columns type (const/ref/range/index/ALL), key, rows, and Extra (`Using index`, `Using filesort`, `Using temporary`); `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` since 8.0
`EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON)` gives machine-readable output for plan diffing in CI

chapters.title: Plan Node Zoo
points: Seq Scan / Full Table Scan: read all pages sequentially. Cheap per page, correct choice for large result fractions
Index Scan: descend the B-tree, then fetch each matching heap row — random I/O, one heap visit per row
Index Only Scan: satisfy the query entirely from index leaves; look for `Heap Fetches: 0`
Bitmap Index Scan + Bitmap Heap Scan: collect matching TIDs into a bitmap, sort by physical page, then read the heap once per page — the middle ground between index and seq scan
Bitmap scans can combine multiple indexes with BitmapAnd/BitmapOr, which is how two single-column indexes cooperate on one query
`Recheck Cond` on a Bitmap Heap Scan is normal; if the bitmap goes lossy the engine re-tests the condition per row
Nested Loop join: for each outer row, probe the inner side — excellent when the outer side is tiny and the inner has an index, catastrophic otherwise
Hash Join: build a hash table on the smaller input, probe with the larger. No index needed; needs memory (watch for `Batches: 4` = spilling to disk)
Merge Join: both inputs sorted on the join key, walked in lockstep — free when indexes already supply the order
Sort node with `Sort Method: external merge Disk: 24MB` means work_mem was exceeded; raise it or supply an index that provides order
Gather / Parallel Seq Scan nodes indicate parallel workers; a seq scan across 8 workers can genuinely beat an index scan

chapters.title: Seq Scan vs Index Scan: The Real Trade-off
points: The comparison is not 'scan all vs scan some' — it's sequential I/O vs random I/O, and sequential reads are ~4-10x cheaper per page
An index scan touching 10% of rows may read nearly every heap page anyway, once at random, and lose badly to one sequential pass
Crossover point is typically somewhere around 5-25% selectivity, depending on row width, correlation, and storage medium
Physical correlation matters: if rows are clustered in index order, an index scan reads few, adjacent pages. Postgres tracks this as `correlation` in pg_stats
`CLUSTER table USING index` physically reorders the heap — a one-time, locking operation that decays as rows are updated
On a small table (a few hundred rows, one or two pages) a seq scan always wins; the planner ignoring your index there is correct
LIMIT flips the math: an ordered index scan can stop after 20 rows while a seq scan + sort must process everything
Bitmap heap scan wins the middle range by converting random heap access into ordered page access
Comparison row — Seq scan: sequential I/O, no index maintenance, parallelizable, cost ∝ table size. Index scan: random I/O, cost ∝ rows matched, provides order
Diagnostic: if EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows a seq scan you dislike, set `enable_seqscan = off` in a session to see the index plan's cost and confirm the planner was right
Never leave enable_* toggles on in production — they're a diagnostic, not a fix

chapters.title: When an Index Hurts
points: Every index multiplies write cost: a table with 8 indexes does 9 structural updates per INSERT, plus WAL/redo for each
HOT updates (Postgres) skip index maintenance only if no indexed column changed and the new tuple fits on the same page — extra indexes make HOT misses more likely
Indexes consume RAM in the buffer pool; a rarely-used index still evicts hot table pages
Low-cardinality indexes (a boolean, a status with 3 values) are usually dead weight — the planner will seq scan anyway
Random-UUID primary keys cause index page splits and write amplification across the whole tree; use UUIDv7/ULID or a sequence instead
Redundant indexes: (a) is fully subsumed by (a, b); duplicates like (a, b) and (a, b) with different names cost writes and buy nothing
Unused indexes accumulate over years — find them with `pg_stat_user_indexes` where idx_scan = 0, or sys.schema_unused_indexes in MySQL
On bulk loads, dropping indexes, loading, then rebuilding is often several times faster than loading with indexes live
Indexes lock: adding one naively takes a write lock. Use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (Postgres) or an online DDL tool — it's slower and can leave an INVALID index on failure
Too many indexes also slows the planner itself, since it must cost more candidate paths
Ratio heuristic: on a write-heavy OLTP table, be suspicious past ~5 indexes; justify each with a real query

chapters.title: Common Mistakes That Silently Disable an Index
points: Wrapping the column in a function: `WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026` cannot use an index on created_at — rewrite as a range `>= '2026-01-01' AND < '2027-01-01'`
Arithmetic on the column: `WHERE price * 1.2 > 100` — move the math to the other side
Implicit type casts: comparing a varchar column to an integer literal, or int to bigint in MySQL, forces a full scan
Leading wildcard: `LIKE '%term'` cannot seek. Use a trigram index (pg_trgm) or a reverse-column index if you truly need suffix search
Case-insensitive search without a matching expression index or a citext/collation-aware index
OR across different columns often defeats a composite index; rewrite as UNION ALL or rely on bitmap OR of two indexes
`NOT IN` / `<>` are unselective by nature — the planner will usually pick a seq scan and be right
Skipping the leading column of a composite index (`WHERE b = ?` on index (a, b)) — the index can only be scanned in full, if at all
Sorting in an order the index doesn't provide, e.g. `ORDER BY a ASC, b ASC` against an index on (a ASC, b DESC)
OFFSET-based pagination degrades linearly: `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000` still walks 100,020 entries. Use keyset pagination: `WHERE (created_at, id) < (?, ?) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20`
Assuming the index exists in production because it exists locally — verify with `\d table` / `SHOW INDEX FROM table`

chapters.title: A Working Diagnostic Method
points: Step 1 — find the query, don't guess: `pg_stat_statements` ordered by total_exec_time, or MySQL's slow query log / performance_schema
Step 2 — optimize total time, not worst single run: a 5ms query run 2M times outranks a 3s report run hourly
Step 3 — run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on realistic production-shaped data; a 1,000-row dev table produces a meaningless plan
Step 4 — locate the node where estimated rows and actual rows diverge most; that subtree is your problem
Step 5 — before adding an index, try ANALYZE. Stale stats are cheaper to fix than a new index to maintain
Step 6 — write the index to match the query shape: equality columns, then range column, then sort columns, then INCLUDE the payload
Step 7 — re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE and compare actual time and buffer reads, not just the plan shape
Step 8 — check `pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan` a week later to confirm the index is actually being used
Watch for hidden regressions: a new index may change the plan of a different query on the same table
Measure index size with `pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('idx_name'))` and weigh it against the buffer pool

chapters.title: Summary & Cheat Sheet
points: Indexes are ordered redundant structures; B+trees dominate because they serve equality, ranges, and ordering with 3-4 page reads
Column order in a composite index is the highest-leverage decision: equality columns first, then one range column, then sort columns
Leftmost prefix rule — an index on (a, b, c) never helps a query that filters only on b or c
Covering indexes eliminate heap access entirely; use INCLUDE for payload columns to keep the key narrow, and VACUUM so index-only scans work
EXPLAIN estimates, EXPLAIN ANALYZE measures. The gap between estimated and actual rows is where bad plans are born
Seq scan wins on large result fractions and small tables; index scan wins on high selectivity and LIMIT; bitmap heap scan owns the middle
Every index taxes writes, RAM, and the planner. Drop what `idx_scan = 0` says nobody uses
Functions, casts, leading wildcards, and OFFSET pagination are the four most common silent index killers
Fix the statistics before you add the index; fix the query before you force the plan
Ordered decision list: is the query slow in aggregate? → EXPLAIN ANALYZE → find estimate/actual gap → ANALYZE → reshape query → then, last, add the narrowest index that matches the query shape
